text.text: <atomic>Owen worked for a laundry service that washed tablecloths for restaurants.</atomic>
<atomic>Owen's manager wanted to know if they were using more bleach than was needed to remove stains from the tablecloths.</atomic>
<atomic>Owen usually washed each load of tablecloths with one cup of bleach.</atomic>
<atomic>He thought that he could reduce the amount of bleach, but he expected that decreasing it by more than 25 percent would make the bleach less effective.</atomic>

<atomic>So, he counted the tablecloths with stains left after washing five loads of tablecloths with one cup of bleach, five loads with ¾ of a cup of bleach, and five loads with ½ of a cup of bleach.</atomic>
<atomic>Then, he checked the percentage of tablecloths in each group that had stains left to see if loads with less bleach had fewer stains removed.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Nina watched her dad sprinkle salt on their driveway before a big snowstorm. She had learned that table salt, or NaCl, prevents ice formation by splitting into two particles and lowering the freezing point of water. She had also heard that calcium chloride, or CaCl<sub>2</sub>, is an even better deicer. She wondered if this might be because CaCl<sub>2</sub> splits into three particles instead of two.</atomic>
<atomic>Nina predicted that the more particles a substance split into when dissolved, the better it would work as a deicer.</atomic>

<atomic>She filled six cups with equal volumes of water. She dissolved sugar, which stays as one particle, in the first two cups. She dissolved NaCl in the next two cups and CaCl<sub>2</sub> in the remaining cups. Each solution had the same concentration. She then left the cups outside in the snowstorm overnight.</atomic>
<atomic>She found that the cups of sugar solution had the most ice in them and the cups of CaCl<sub>2</sub> solution had the least.</atomic>
<atomic>She decided that she was correct in predicting that substances that break into more particles make better deicers.</atomic>
<atomic>She shared the results with her chemistry teacher, and he confirmed that a substance's ability to change water's freezing point is impacted by how many particles it breaks into.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>One afternoon, Stacy was making tea with her father. As Stacy stirred her tea, the metal spoon quickly became too hot to hold. Her dad suggested that she use a wooden spoon instead.</atomic>
<atomic>Stacy was curious if the type of material a spoon is made from affects how much it heats up when placed in hot water for a short amount of time.</atomic>
<atomic>She remembered hearing that metal conducts heat well and reasoned that the metal spoon would heat up more than a plastic or wooden spoon.</atomic>

<atomic>Stacy filled a large bowl with hot water. She then placed a metal spoon, a plastic spoon, and a wooden spoon into the bowl of water at the same time. After one minute, she used a thermometer to measure the temperature of each spoon's handle.</atomic>

<atomic>Stacy recorded the temperatures and found that the metal spoon had heated up the most, the plastic spoon was warm but comfortable to hold, and the wooden spoon remained close to room temperature.</atomic>
<atomic>She concluded that the type of material does affect how much a spoon heats up over a period of time.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Karen's chemistry class had just gone over Charles's law, which states that a gas expands when its temperature increases. She wondered if she could see this effect with balloons.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that a balloon would shrink when cooled down and expand when heated up.</atomic>

<atomic>To see if she was right, she inflated six balloons and measured the circumference of each one. She then put two in the freezer, kept two at room temperature, and warmed two up with a hair dryer. Then she measured each balloon's circumference again.</atomic>
<atomic>She found that the balloons that were in the freezer shrank, the ones kept at room temperature remained the same size, and the ones that were heated expanded.</atomic>
<atomic>Karen decided that her prediction was correct.</atomic>
<atomic>A few weeks later, her brother started crying because his balloon had deflated slightly, so Karen showed him the trick of warming up the balloon to "revive" it.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Jacob was playing with a rubber band and wondered how the stretchiness of flexible materials might vary.</atomic>
<atomic>Jacob thought that rubber bands would stretch more than other common flexible materials, like plastic wrap or silicone, because they feel more elastic and springy.</atomic>

<atomic>Jacob collected a few items: a rubber band, a piece of plastic wrap, and a silicone baking mat. He cut the rubber band to make a strip and then cut similarly sized pieces from the other items. He then gently pulled on the two ends of the rubber band until it reached its limit, and his sister measured its length. Jacob and his sister repeated this with the other two materials.</atomic>
<atomic>They noticed that the rubber band stretched a lot, the plastic wrap stretched less, and the silicone mat stretched very little.</atomic>
<atomic>Jacob determined that rubber is more elastic than plastic wrap and silicone, which allows it to stretch the most.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>While washing his hands at his aunt's house, Malik noticed that the soap didn't seem to lather as much as it did at his own house.</atomic>
<atomic>He remembered hearing that "hard water" has a higher mineral content than "soft water."</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered if the soap lathered less at his aunt's house due to the water having a higher mineral content.</atomic>

<atomic>When he got home, Malik filled 12 identical bottles with the same volume of distilled water. He added nothing to 4 of the bottles, one teaspoon of Epsom salt to 4 of the bottles, and two teaspoons of Epsom salt to the remaining 4 bottles. After adding a drop of soap to the first bottle, he put his thumb over the opening and shook it to make bubbles. He then used a ruler to measure the height of the bubbles.</atomic>

<atomic>Once he had repeated the procedure with all of the bottles, Malik calculated the average height of the bubbles for each type of water. He found that the bottles containing only distilled water had the tallest column of bubbles, and the bottles with two teaspoons of Epsom salt added had the shortest.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that soap lathers less in hard water than it does in soft water.</atomic>
<atomic>When Malik told his aunt about the experiment, she confirmed that her house does have hard water.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>While washing his hands at his aunt's house, Malik noticed that the soap didn't seem to lather as much as it did at his own house.</atomic>
<atomic>He remembered hearing that "hard water" has a higher mineral content than "soft water."</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered if the soap lathered less at his aunt's house due to the water having a higher mineral content.</atomic>

<atomic>When he got home, Malik filled 12 identical bottles with the same volume of distilled water. He added nothing to 4 of the bottles, one teaspoon of Epsom salt to 4 of the bottles, and two teaspoons of Epsom salt to the remaining 4 bottles. After adding a drop of soap to the first bottle, he put his thumb over the opening and shook it to make bubbles. He then used a ruler to measure the height of the bubbles.</atomic>

<atomic>Once he had repeated the procedure with all of the bottles, Malik calculated the average height of the bubbles for each type of water. He found that the bottles containing only distilled water had the tallest column of bubbles, and the bottles with two teaspoons of Epsom salt added had the shortest.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that soap lathers less in hard water than it does in soft water.</atomic>
<atomic>When Malik told his aunt about the experiment, she confirmed that her house does have hard water.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Zane was helping his mom make pickles. As he was adding salt to water to make brine, he recalled that sugar dissolves better in hot water than in cold.</atomic>
<atomic>Zane thought that the temperature of the water might also affect how well salt would dissolve.</atomic>

<atomic>To test this idea, Zane filled nine identical glasses with equal volumes of water. He filled three with water that was heated on the stovetop, three with water at room temperature, and the remaining three with chilled water. Then he added a tablespoon of salt to each glass and stirred the water. Zane continued to add one tablespoon at a time to each glass until the salt no longer dissolved.</atomic>

<atomic>He calculated the average amount of dissolved salt for each group. He found that the glasses containing chilled water dissolved the least amount of salt, and the glasses containing hot water dissolved the most.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that the temperature of the water does indeed affect the solubility of salt.</atomic>
<atomic>He asked his mom why this was the case, and she explained that the warmer water molecules move faster, which helps them break apart the salt crystals.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Julie was excited to try out oil painting as a new hobby. As she gathered her supplies, she wondered what she should use to clean her brushes. Some artists simply used water, while others recommended mineral spirits. Which cleaner was best for her paint?</atomic>
<atomic>Julie remembered the principle "like dissolves like" from science class.</atomic>
<atomic>She reasoned that water, a polar substance, would dissolve other polar substances. Since oils are nonpolar, they require a nonpolar solvent—like mineral spirits.</atomic>

<atomic>She decided to test her idea by taking three cups of mineral spirits and putting an identical brush with black oil paint in each one. She then filled three more cups with water and duplicated the procedure with them.</atomic>
<atomic>Three days later, she checked the cups. The mineral spirits had turned dark and cloudy, while the water was much clearer, with most of the paint still on the brushes.</atomic>
<atomic>She concluded that mineral spirits are the best cleaner for oil paints since they are both nonpolar.</atomic>
<atomic>She shared her results on an art blog.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>On a cold winter morning, Amy opened her door to come in from a snowy day. She was struck by how much colder the metal doorknob felt than the wooden door.</atomic>
<atomic>If they were both out in the same temperature, why did one feel colder?</atomic>
<atomic>She thought that the wood might absorb heat from the sun better than the metal, which raised the temperature of the door.</atomic>

<atomic>To test her idea, she got two wooden cubes and two metal cubes of the same size. She put one of each type of cube in the shade, and another of each type in the sun. Three hours later, she used an infrared thermometer to measure the temperature of each sample.</atomic>
<atomic>To her surprise, the metal and the wood that were left in the sun were the same temperature!</atomic>
<atomic>She decided her idea was wrong—she had predicted that the wooden cube left in the sun would be warmer than the metal cube in the sun.</atomic>
<atomic>Instead, the materials must somehow feel different even though they have the same temperature.</atomic>

<atomic>She asked her chemistry teacher about it, and he explained that metals have a lower specific heat. That makes them feel colder than wood at low temperatures and hotter than wood at high temperatures.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Shelley was getting ready to go for a hike. In order to stay hydrated, she dissolved an electrolyte tablet in a glass of water.</atomic>
<atomic>As she waited for the tablet to fully dissolve, she wondered how she could speed up the reaction rate.</atomic>
<atomic>Shelley predicted that warmer water would cause electrolyte tablets to dissolve more quickly.</atomic>

<atomic>She filled four cups with equal volumes of water. She warmed two of the cups in the microwave and left the other two cups at room temperature. She dropped one tablet into each cup at the same time and used a timer to track how long each tablet took to stop fizzing.</atomic>
<atomic>She averaged the times from each group and noticed that the warmer water almost cut the fizz time in half!</atomic>
<atomic>Shelley concluded that the temperature of the water does affect the reaction rate of electrolyte tablets.</atomic>
<atomic>She shared her results with her hiking group.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Johnny was learning about liquids in chemistry class. His teacher explained that when a liquid is heated to its boiling point, the particles begin to separate from one another.</atomic>
<atomic>Johnny was curious if a liquid's boiling point could help you predict its cohesion, or how much its particles tend to stick together.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that liquids with high boiling points must be very cohesive.</atomic>
<atomic>Johnny looked up the boiling points of three liquids: rubbing alcohol (80°C), water (100°C), and vegetable oil (300°C).</atomic>

<atomic>Then he tested the cohesion of each liquid by placing drops of each one on a penny. The more cohesive a liquid is, the more drops can fit without spilling off. He added drops of rubbing alcohol one by one and counted how many drops could fit on the penny until it spilled off. He dried the penny off and tried it twice more, then averaged the three values. He then repeated the procedure with water and vegetable oil.</atomic>
<atomic>When he compared the averaged values, he found that vegetable oil held the fewest drops on the penny—the opposite of what he expected!</atomic>
<atomic>He now thought that there must be more to boiling point than just cohesion.</atomic>

<atomic>He asked his chemistry teacher, and she explained that although cohesion influences boiling point, other factors such as molecular weight and the shape of the molecules affect it as well.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Emma was learning about liquids in chemistry class.</atomic>
<atomic>She wondered what happens when liquids freeze—do they get more or less dense?</atomic>
<atomic>Emma already knew that ice floats to the top of water because ice is less dense, so she reasoned that liquids must get less dense when they freeze.</atomic>

<atomic>Emma filled two small cups with olive oil and two small cups with white vinegar. She put one cup of each liquid in the freezer and kept the other cups on the counter. The next morning, Emma removed the cups from the freezer. She put a piece of the solid olive oil into the liquid olive oil and a piece of the solid vinegar into the liquid vinegar.</atomic>
<atomic>To her surprise, both solids sank!</atomic>
<atomic>Emma realized that water must be unusual, and that most liquids must get denser when they freeze.</atomic>
<atomic>When she told her teacher about her experiment, her teacher confirmed that most liquids do get more dense when they freeze.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Aaron worked in a candy factory.</atomic>
<atomic>He was making a new recipe for fudge that called for cooling the fudge at room temperature instead of at the usual cold temperature.</atomic>

<atomic>He found that fudge cooled at 40°F was less grainy than fudge cooled at 75°F.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Logan worked at a cafe.</atomic>
<atomic>Each morning, he made syrup from granulated sugar and water.</atomic>
<atomic>One day, Logan noticed a bag of superfine sugar on the shelf.</atomic>
<atomic>He read online that superfine sugar crystals are smaller than granulated sugar crystals.</atomic>
<atomic>He was curious about whether one type of sugar would dissolve in water more quickly than the other.</atomic>
<atomic>Logan predicted that superfine sugar would dissolve more slowly than granulated sugar because there are more individual crystals per gram of superfine sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>He added one gram of granulated sugar to one cup of water and one gram of superfine sugar to another, then noted which sugar type dissolved first.</atomic>
<atomic>He repeated his test six times and found that the superfine sugar always dissolved faster than the granulated sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>Logan decided to redo his investigation with powdered sugar and superfine sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that because finer sugars dissolve faster, the powdered sugar would dissolve faster than the superfine sugar.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Devin learned in science class that oil and water do not mix together. His teacher proved this by adding both substances to a container and shaking it. Devin noticed that the oil floated to the top of the container after it had sat untouched for a while.</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered, "Could a thick enough oil layer prevent the water from evaporating?"</atomic>
<atomic>He guessed that the thicker the oil layer was, the less water would evaporate because the oil would act as a barrier and stop water molecules from escaping into the air.</atomic>

<atomic>Devin set up nine identical cups and filled each one with an equal amount of water. In the first three cups, he added a thin layer of vegetable oil, just enough to cover the surface. In the next three cups, he added a thicker layer of oil. He did not add any oil to the remaining cups. He left them all on the counter for three days. Then Devin measured the water level in each cup and calculated the average for each group.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the water level was the lowest in the cup with no oil and the highest in the cup with a thick layer of oil.</atomic>
<atomic>He concluded that a thicker layer of oil does indeed reduce water evaporation more effectively than a thin layer.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>One summer day, Christy was outside helping her dad spray paint some handles for their kitchen cabinets. When they finished, her dad asked her to take the spray paint inside, because leaving it in the hot sun could cause the canisters to explode. He explained that raising a gas's temperature also raises its pressure. Christy wondered how she could test this relationship.</atomic>
<atomic>Not wanting to cause any explosions, she decided to test it with her dad's car tires.</atomic>
<atomic>She predicted that the tire pressure would increase after he drove, since the tires would warm up on the road.</atomic>
<atomic>She measured the pressure of each tire on her dad's car before he drove it to work. When he came home, she measured the pressure again.</atomic>
<atomic>She was excited to see that each tire's pressure had increased!</atomic>
<atomic>She concluded that she was correct in predicting that driving raises the pressure in car tires.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Keegan was washing dishes after dinner. As he used detergent to clean oils off the plates, he was reminded of how his chemistry teacher said detergents worked: by disrupting surface tension.</atomic>
<atomic>Did that mean that detergents kept liquids from holding together?</atomic>
<atomic>Keegan predicted that as more detergent was added to a liquid, the liquid would hold together less well.</atomic>

<atomic>He filled four cups with the same amount of water. He mixed one drop of detergent in the first cup, two drops in the second, and three drops in the third. He did not add any detergent to the fourth cup. Next, he took four quarters. He added one drop of plain water at a time onto one of the quarters until the water spilled off. He counted the drops and repeated the experiment with the remaining quarters and solutions.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that plain water took the most drops to spill off, while the water with three drops of detergent took the least.</atomic>
<atomic>He determined that he was correct in predicting that detergent made liquids hold together less well.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Erica loves making lemonade with fresh-squeezed lemon juice and water. She noticed that after a day or two in the fridge, her lemonade would turn brown and lose its fresh taste.</atomic>

<atomic>While looking at the ingredient list on a store-bought lemonade bottle, she saw that it included sugar and citric acid. Erica wondered if adding these ingredients to her homemade lemonade would help preserve its color and freshness.</atomic>

<atomic>To test this idea, Erica prepared six identical bottles of freshly squeezed lemon juice from the same batch. She added one teaspoon of sugar to two of the bottles and one teaspoon of powdered citric acid to the next two. She added nothing to the remaining bottles. Then she labeled the bottles and placed them in the fridge.</atomic>
<atomic>After three days, she observed that the bottles with plain lemon juice and the ones with sugar had all turned brown, while the ones with citric acid stayed bright and fresh.</atomic>
<atomic>Erica now predicted that citric acid was more effective than sugar at preserving lemonade's color and freshness.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Ben had a hydrangea plant that produced blue flowers. He moved his plant from a pot to a planter bed in his yard, and the next time the plant flowered, the flowers were pink!</atomic>
<atomic>He tested the soils and found that the pH, or acidity, differed between the pot and the planter bed.</atomic>
<atomic>This led him to wonder if soil pH could affect the color of hydrangea flowers.</atomic>
<atomic>Ben filled five pots with soil with a pH of 5.0 and another five with soil with a pH of 6.5. He planted six hydrangea seeds in each pot.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the plants grown in pH 6.5 soil bloomed pink, while those grown in pH 5.0 soil bloomed blue.</atomic>
<atomic>Ben deduced that soil pH influences hydrangea flower color.</atomic>
<atomic>He shared his results on his favorite gardening blog.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Deb was a deejay who used a bubble machine at her events.</atomic>
<atomic>She wanted to know how to make the bubbles last longer.</atomic>
<atomic>She read in a book that bubbles burst because the liquid that makes up the bubbles evaporates.</atomic>
<atomic>She knew that warm liquids evaporate faster than cold liquids.</atomic>
<atomic>So, Deb expected that the temperature of the bubble solution could affect how long the bubbles lasted, with colder bubbles lasting longer.</atomic>
<atomic>Deb heated six bottles of bubble solution to 110°F, kept six bottles at 75°F, and cooled six bottles to 40°F, and then she measured how long bubbles from each of the bottles lasted.</atomic>
<atomic>Because the bubbles from the colder solution lasted longer than bubbles from the other solutions, Deb reasoned that temperature does affect bubble lifespan.</atomic>
<atomic>For her next deejay event, she iced the bubble solution before she loaded it into the bubble machine.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>After a severe ice storm, Justin wondered how he could melt ice on the sidewalk.</atomic>
<atomic>He had heard that sand, when heated by the sun, could melt ice.</atomic>
<atomic>So, Justin got twenty ice cubes that were equal in weight.</atomic>
<atomic>He sprinkled sand on half the ice cubes and left the other half unsanded.</atomic>
<atomic>He placed all the cubes outside for one hour and then brushed off the sand and reweighed them.</atomic>
<atomic>Justin calculated the average weight of each type of cube to see if the sanded cubes melted more than the unsanded cubes.</atomic>
<atomic>He decided that sand did not speed up melting, since the two types of ice cubes were similar weights.</atomic>
<atomic>Then, he read that salt makes ice melt at a cooler temperature.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that because the melting temperature would be lowered, ice cubes would melt faster if he applied salt to them.</atomic>

text.text: <atomic>Jackson loves doing experiments in his kitchen, especially ones that involve fun reactions. One day, he mixed baking soda and vinegar to create fizzy foam.</atomic>
<atomic>He wondered if the diameter of the container where he mixed the ingredients affected how high the foam could rise.</atomic>
<atomic>Jackson thought that the diameter of the container shouldn't matter; it is the ingredients themselves that determine the height of the foam.</atomic>

<atomic>Jackson found three containers with different diameters: a narrow glass, a wider jar, and an even wider bowl. He added the same amount of baking soda and vinegar to each container. Jackson then used a ruler to measure the height of the foam produced.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the foam in the wide bowl was the shortest, while the foam in the narrow glass was the tallest.</atomic>
<atomic>He now predicted that a taller, narrower container allowed the foam to rise higher because it provided less surface area for the foam to spread out.</atomic>
<atomic>The next week, Jackson shared his results with his science club at school.</atomic>

<atomic>Cole knew that adding salt to water would cause the water to reach a higher temperature before it boiled.</atomic>
<atomic>Because pasta should cook faster at a higher temperature, Cole speculated that the added salt would make the pasta cook more quickly.</atomic>
<atomic>Cole made four pots of pasta with salted water and another four pots with unsalted water.</atomic>
<atomic>He compared the amount of time it took the pasta to cook to see if it cooked faster in pots with salt.</atomic>
<atomic>His results showed that although the water from the salted pots boiled at a slightly hotter temperature, the pasta cooked at similar rates in all the pots.</atomic>
<atomic>He discussed the results of the experiment with his coworkers.</atomic>
<atomic>They decided not to bother adding salt to the pasta water.</atomic>

contents.text: Scientific inquiry is a process used by scientists to answer questions and solve problems. The steps of the process do not always need to be performed in a fixed order. Depending on the questions they are exploring, scientists may repeat, skip, or reorder steps.
Scientific inquiry often involves the following steps:

pieces.text: Scientists use observations and background knowledge to pose a question about a scientific problem.
Scientists propose possible explanations to a question. A good hypothesis is based on sound logic, is supported by background research, and can be tested.
Scientists collect data by conducting experiments or making observations. The data may support or refute their hypothesis.
Scientists examine their data for trends and patterns, often using charts, graphs, or tables.
Scientists determine whether their data supports their hypothesis. If their hypothesis was not supported, they may
by making a new prediction.
Whether or not their hypothesis was supported, scientists explain their investigation to others.

text.text: <atomic>Eddie likes to make rock candy to share with his friends.</atomic>
<atomic>He normally makes rock candy using white sugar but wondered if he could make larger sugar crystals using pure cane sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>He predicted that pure cane sugar would make the largest crystals, since it was a more pure form of sugar.</atomic>

<atomic>Eddie set up 12 glass jars with a stick and hot water. He added white sugar to 6 jars and pure cane sugar to the other 6. After one week, Eddie measured the size of the sugar crystals in each jar.</atomic>
<atomic>He found that the rock candy made with white sugar had larger crystals than those made with pure cane sugar.</atomic>
<atomic>He then predicted that smaller sugar granules would lead to larger sugar crystals.</atomic>

He then added a drop of soap to each bottle and shook each one to make bubbles. Finally, he used a ruler to measure how thick the bubble layer was in each bottle.

mainText.text: As Jenny was helping her dad cook, she noticed that salted water seemed to take longer to boil than plain tap water. Her dad explained that dissolving a substance in water can raise the water's boiling point. Jenny reasoned that since salt water has a higher boiling point than tap water, it should also have a higher freezing point. To test her idea, Jenny poured an equal amount of water into six cups. She added nothing to the first two cups, one teaspoon of salt to each of the second two cups, and two teaspoons of salt to each of the final two cups. Then, she placed a thermometer in each cup and put the cups in the freezer. Every 15 minutes, she observed the temperatures and checked whether the water in each cup had frozen. To Jenny's surprise, the water with the most salt had the lowest freezing point!
